newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain confident world will back Zaire aid force.
newsitem.headline: Spain confident world will back Zaire aid force.

text.p: Spain was confident on Friday a plan to send troops to Zaire to open safe corridors for starving refugees would eventually win U.S. and international backing but acknowledged it would come too late for hundreds of thousands.
The government sent two planeloads of medicine and food for the refugees to Kinshasa and Nairobi on Friday but a Foreign Ministry spokesman was unsure the aid would reach the war zone.

A Franco-Spanish proposal to send at least 5,000 troops to eastern Zaire to open humanitarian corridors for distribution of food, water and medicine has yet to receive the international backing the two European countries are seeking.
"The plan is going to work. The U.S. and international community will send troops," said the spokesman, who asked not to be named.
"But it will be too late anyhow. Now people are starving, they are dying from hunger. When these troops reach Kindu, it will be too late. Hundreds of thousands will be dead at that time."
He said he hoped the force would be able to prevent the deaths of hundreds of thousands more refugees caught in fighting between Zaire's army and ethnic Tutsis rebels backed by Rwanda.

The complex multi-sided war in eastern Zaire has cut off more than one million Rwandan refugees from the outside world and also driven more and more Zaireans to hunger. International aid workers in the area have called repeatedly for urgent action to avert a massive humanitarian disaster.
Spain and France have said their plan will not go forward without support from the United States, the U.N. and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU). They have so far failed to win that backing.
European Union development aid ministers met in Brussels on Thursday but failed to back military intervention. Instead, they put the onus on the U.N. Security Council to lead any action.

British Prime Minister John Major signalled on Friday that his country might send troops. Major was at a summit in Bordeaux, France with the chief advocate of military intervention, French President Jacques Chirac.

"(The French-Spanish plan) has been well received by the international community, the U.N. and by the European Union but no other country has pronounced they are going to send troops," the Spanish spokesman said.
One encouraging sign was a statement by Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko in France on Wednesday that he would back a troop deployment.
Spain and France want to send in a multinational force of at least 5,000, to be replaced gradually by African troops.

Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes on Thursday condemned the world community and African regional leaders for what he said were years of neglecting the problems of central Africa which led to the latest crisis.
South Africa suspended arms sales to Rwanda on Wednesday and indicated it would contribute troops to an international force for Zaire if the United Nations and the OAU asked it to do so.
South Africa's decision to suspend the arms contract followed reports that Rwandan forces were taking part in the fighting in eastern Zaire between rival Tutsi and Hutu tribes.
South African President Nelson Mandela has accepted a request from Mobutu to play a major diplomatic role in peace efforts in central Africa. But it was unclear what he would do to help end fighting.
Spain sent two transport planes to the area early on Friday loaded with medicines, food, tents, water purification supplies and vaccines destined for Red Cross depositories.
"We don't know if (the aid) will be allowed in," the Foreign Ministry spokesman said. "The problem is. will it reach Goma or Bukavu?"
